# Multiple Linear Regression *** We often want to know the relationship between one outcome variable $\hat{y}_{i}$ and multiple explanatory variables. This builds on [Simple Regression](02_15_SimpleRegression.qmd), which related $\hat{y}_{i}$ to a single $\hat{x}_{i}$. *Multiple linear regression* fits a single linear model to several explanatory variables at once, and asks how each one moves the outcome while holding the others fixed. This chapter asks three questions. * How is $\hat{y}$ associated with each explanatory variable, holding the others fixed? * *Multiple regression coefficients*: OLS picks one coefficient $\hat{b}_{k}$ per explanatory variable, with the same objective as [simple regression](02_15_SimpleRegression.qmd#model-and-objective). * How sure are we? * *Bootstrap standard errors*: these assess sampling variability, with the same recipe as the [slope](02_15_SimpleRegression.qmd#bootstrap). * *Joint bootstrap distribution and permutation $F$-test*: these assess several coefficients at once. The test shuffles the outcome, the same recipe as earlier [permutation tests](02_12_TwoGroups.qmd#permutation-tests). * *Adjusted R-squared*: this is a new model assessment check that does not reward adding pure noise, unlike [R-squared](02_15_SimpleRegression.qmd#goodness-of-fit). * What do the coefficients mean? * *Correctly specified and misspecified simulations*: these show that coefficients center on the true values when the data are truly linear. Otherwise, OLS returns the best linear approximation. For historical reasons, we start by fitting a linear model to data. ## The Linear Model #### **Model and Objective** {-} With several explanatory variables we need a rule for picking one specific coefficient vector out of the infinite candidates that almost fit the data. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} The *linear model* with $K$ cardinal explanatory variables $\hat{x}_{i1}, \hat{x}_{i2}, \ldots, \hat{x}_{iK}$ and sample residual $\hat{e}_{i}$ is $$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}_{i} &= b_{0} + b_{1} \hat{x}_{i1}+ b_{2} \hat{x}_{i2}+\ldots+b_{K} \hat{x}_{iK} + \hat{e}_{i} = \sum_{k=0}^{K} b_{k} \hat{x}_{ik} + \hat{e}_{i}. \end{aligned}$$ Note that $\hat{x}_{i0}=1$ in the summation. The coefficients $b_{k}$ are trial values, and each $\hat{e}_{i}$ is computed from the observed data for those values. *Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)* picks the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals $$\min_{b_{0}, b_{1}, \ldots, b_{K}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{e}_{i}^2.$$ ::: OLS is useful when you want one coefficient per explanatory variable summarizing its partial relationship with $\hat{y}$ holding the others fixed; it is the workhorse of linear modeling because the minimization has a closed-form solution via matrix calculations (see [these notes](https://jrnold.github.io/intro-methods-notes/ols-in-matrix-form.html) for a detailed derivation). The solution yields the best fitting coefficient vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=(\hat{b}_{0} ~~ \hat{b}_{1} ~~... ~~ \hat{b}_{K})$. Plugging it into the model gives the fitted value for observation $i$: $$\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \hat{b}_{k} \hat{x}_{ik}.$$ At these fitted coefficients, $\hat{e}_{i} = \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ is the observed value minus the fitted value. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE # Lab data: 3294 US workers # wage is the hourly wage in 1980 dollars # school and exper are years of schooling and of work experience # sex is a factor with levels female and male data(Wages1, package='Ecdat') xy_hat <- Wages1 # Fit a multiple regression of wage on school and exper reg <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat) coef(reg) ## (Intercept) school exper ## -2.4766831 0.5992289 0.1572607 # With experience fixed, a year of schooling goes with 60 cents more an hour. # With schooling fixed, a year of experience goes with 16 cents more an hour. # Compare with schooling alone and with the raw correlations coef(lm(wage ~ school, data=xy_hat)) ## (Intercept) school ## -0.7225066 0.5571617 cor(xy_hat[, c('wage', 'school', 'exper')]) ## wage school exper ## wage 1.00000000 0.2824925 0.05138051 ## school 0.28249249 1.0000000 -0.19356533 ## exper 0.05138051 -0.1935653 1.00000000 # Experience barely correlates with wages on its own, about 0.05. # Its coefficient is still clearly positive once schooling is held fixed. # Schooling and experience are negatively correlated, about -0.19. # So holding experience fixed raises the schooling coefficient, 0.557 to 0.599. ``` ::: :::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"} Add `sex` as a third explanatory variable: run `lm(wage ~ school + exper + sex, data=xy_hat)` and compare the coefficients to those above. R enters this two-level factor as one 0/1 dummy variable, shown as `sexmale` in the output. Which coefficients change the most? Does the sign of any coefficient change? What does this tell you about the relationship between the explanatory variables? ::: #### **Goodness of fit** {-} To measure how well the model fits the data, we can again plot our predictions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Limits near 20 dollars leave out the 16 largest wages plot(xy_hat$wage, predict(reg), pch=16, col=grey(0, .1), xlim=c(0, 20), ylim=c(0, 20), main=NA, xlab='Observed hourly wage (1980 dollars)', ylab='Predicted hourly wage (1980 dollars)') abline(a=0, b=1, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Predicted wages span only about 2 to 8 dollars, so the cloud lies flat. # A close fit would hug the dashed line. # Here R-squared is about 0.09, so most of the wage variation goes unexplained. ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Repeat the plot with `USArrests`, regressing `Murder` on `Assault` and `UrbanPop`. How close do the points sit to the dashed line, compared to the figure above? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Second dataset: arrests per 100,000 residents in the 50 US states, 1973 # UrbanPop is the percent of the population living in urban areas xy2_hat <- USArrests reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault+UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat) coef(reg2) ## (Intercept) Assault UrbanPop ## 3.20715340 0.04390995 -0.04451047 plot(xy2_hat$Murder, predict(reg2), pch=16, col=grey(0, .5), main=NA, xlab='Observed Murder', ylab='Predicted Murder') abline(a=0, b=1, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Predictions track the observed values much more closely. # R-squared is about 0.66. ``` ::: ::: #### **Adjusted $\hat{R}^2$** {-} The ordinary *coefficient of determination* is the share of variance the model explains, $\hat{R}^2 = \frac{\hat{\text{ESS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}}=1-\frac{\hat{\text{RSS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}}$. Adding extra regressors can mechanically raise the ordinary $\hat{R}^2$ even when the new variables are pure noise, so we need a fit measure that does not reward including junk. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} The *adjusted $\hat{R}^2$* multiplies the unexplained share by a factor that grows with the number of explanatory variables $K$, $$\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-\frac{n-1}{n-K-1}(1-\hat{R}^2),$$ where $K+1$ counts all estimated coefficients including the intercept (so $K+1=3$ for a model with two explanatory variables). ::: The *adjusted $\hat{R}^2$* is useful for comparing models with different numbers of regressors on the same dataset: it rises when an added variable improves fit by more than random noise would. The penalty $(n-1)/(n-K-1)$ is the only thing distinguishing it from the unadjusted version, and it can in fact go negative if the model fits worse than a constant. :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Suppose $n=50$, $K=2$, and $\hat{R}^2=0.70$. Then $$\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \frac{49}{47}(1-0.70) = 1 - 1.043 \times 0.30 \approx 0.687.$$ The adjustment reduces $\hat{R}^2$ slightly. With more covariates the penalty grows: if instead $K=9$, then $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \frac{49}{40}(0.30) = 1 - 0.3675 = 0.6325$. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE # Add pure-noise covariates to a copy, so later chunks still use the original data ksims <- 1:30 xy_noise_hat <- xy_hat for(k in ksims){ xy_noise_hat[, paste0('R', k)] <- runif(nrow(xy_hat), 0, 20) } R2_sim <- rep(NA, length(ksims)) R2adj_sim <- rep(NA, length(ksims)) for(k in ksims){ rvars <- c('school', 'exper', paste0('R', 1:k)) rvars2 <- paste0(rvars, collapse='+') reg_k <- lm( paste0('wage ~ ', rvars2), data=xy_noise_hat) R2_sim[k] <- summary(reg_k)$r.squared R2adj_sim[k] <- summary(reg_k)$adj.r.squared } # Zoom in on the y-axis, since noise moves R-squared little with 3294 workers plot.new() plot.window(xlim=c(0, 30), ylim=range(R2_sim, R2adj_sim)) points(ksims, R2_sim) points(ksims, R2adj_sim, pch=16) axis(1) axis(2) mtext(expression(R^2), 2, line=3) mtext('Additional Random Covariates', 1, line=3) legend('topleft', horiz=TRUE, legend=c('Unadjusted', 'Adjusted'), pch=c(1, 16)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Pure noise lifts the unadjusted R-squared from about 0.092 to about 0.102. # The adjusted R-squared stays near 0.09. ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Repeat the simulation with `USArrests`. How does the number of rows change what noise can do to the unadjusted $\hat{R}^2$? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Second dataset: arrests per 100,000 residents in the 50 US states, 1973 # Its 50 rows are far fewer than the 3294 workers in the lab data. xy2_hat <- USArrests # Add pure-noise covariates to a copy, so later chunks still use the original data ksims <- 1:30 xy2_noise_hat <- xy2_hat for(k in ksims){ xy2_noise_hat[, paste0('R', k)] <- runif(nrow(xy2_hat), 0, 20) } R2_sim2 <- rep(NA, length(ksims)) R2adj_sim2 <- rep(NA, length(ksims)) for(k in ksims){ rvars <- c('Assault', 'UrbanPop', paste0('R', 1:k)) rvars2 <- paste0(rvars, collapse='+') reg2_k <- lm( paste0('Murder ~ ', rvars2), data=xy2_noise_hat) R2_sim2[k] <- summary(reg2_k)$r.squared R2adj_sim2[k] <- summary(reg2_k)$adj.r.squared } plot.new() plot.window(xlim=c(0, 30), ylim=c(0, 1)) points(ksims, R2_sim2) points(ksims, R2adj_sim2, pch=16) axis(1) axis(2) mtext(expression(R^2), 2, line=3) mtext('Additional Random Covariates', 1, line=3) legend('topleft', horiz=TRUE, legend=c('Unadjusted', 'Adjusted'), pch=c(1, 16)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # With only 50 states, noise lifts the unadjusted R-squared a lot. # It climbs from about 0.66 to about 0.9. # The adjusted R-squared falls to about 0.48 before ending near 0.7. # With so few rows per covariate, chance fits can move it a lot. ``` ::: ::: ## Variability Estimates and Hypothesis Tests Above, we computed the coefficient vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ for a particular sample: $\hat{x}_{i1}, \hat{x}_{i2}, \ldots, \hat{y}_{i}$. We now seek to know how much the estimator $\mathbf{B}$ varies from sample to sample. I.e., $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is our estimate, and we want the standard errors $\text{SE}(B_{k})$ of its individual coefficient estimators. We write the estimated standard errors as $\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{k})$ and compute them using the same data-driven methods introduced previously. As before, we can also conduct independent hypothesis tests using t-values. However, we can also conduct *joint tests* that account for interdependencies in our estimates. For example, to test whether two coefficients both equal $0$, we bootstrap the joint distribution of coefficients. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE # Bootstrap SEs of all three coefficients jointly: resample rows of the # dataset with replacement, refit lm, and store the coefficient vector. boot_coefs <- matrix(NA, nrow=399, ncol=3) for(b in seq(nrow(boot_coefs))){ b_id <- sample( nrow(xy_hat), replace=TRUE) xy_boot <- xy_hat[b_id, ] reg_b <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_boot) boot_coefs[b, ] <- coef(reg_b) } colnames(boot_coefs) <- names(coef(reg)) # The bootstrap SE is just the standard deviation across replications apply(boot_coefs, 2, sd) ## (Intercept) school exper ## 0.48176469 0.03443589 0.02451051 # The SEs are about 0.034 for school and 0.025 for exper. # Both are small next to the coefficients, 0.599 and 0.157. ``` ::: #### **Joint Hypothesis Tests** {-} When coefficient estimates are correlated, testing them one at a time can miss dependencies that a joint test captures. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} A *joint hypothesis test* asks whether several coefficients are simultaneously consistent with a stated null (e.g., $\beta_{1} = \beta_{2} = 0$). The bootstrap above approximates the joint sampling distribution of $\mathbf{B}$, so we can read off the joint distribution rather than just the marginals. ::: A *joint test* is useful when two coefficients move together across resamples: pooling the evidence into one test reflects the actual joint uncertainty, whereas two separate $t$-tests would either double-count or miss the dependence entirely. A joint test is also preferable to tests of single coefficients when multicollinearity makes the individual coefficient estimates highly variable [@BelsleyEtAl1980; @fox2020]. The plot below visualizes the bootstrap joint distribution of two coefficients, where each point is one bootstrap replicate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE # The joint distribution of the exper and school coefficients boot_coef_df <- as.data.frame(cbind( ID=seq(nrow(boot_coefs)), boot_coefs)) fig <- plotly::plot_ly(boot_coef_df, type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers', x = ~ exper, y = ~ school, text = ~ paste(' bootstrap dataset: ', ID, '', '
Coef. exper :', round(exper, 3), '
Coef. school :', round(school, 3), '
Coef. Intercept :', round(`(Intercept)`, 3)), hoverinfo='text', showlegend=FALSE, marker=list( color='rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)')) fig <- plotly::layout(fig, showlegend=FALSE, title='Joint Bootstrap Distribution of Coefficients', xaxis = list(title='exper Coefficient'), yaxis = list(title='school Coefficient')) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The cloud tilts up slightly: the two coefficients tend to move together. # Their correlation across replicates is about 0.2. ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Repeat the joint bootstrap with `USArrests`, regressing `Murder` on `Assault` and `UrbanPop`. Do the two coefficients move together in the same direction as in the figure above? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Second dataset: arrests per 100,000 residents in the 50 US states, 1973 xy2_hat <- USArrests reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault+UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat) # Bootstrap SEs of all three coefficients jointly: resample rows of the # dataset with replacement, refit lm, and store the coefficient vector. boot_coefs2 <- matrix(NA, nrow=399, ncol=3) for(b in seq(nrow(boot_coefs2))){ b_id <- sample( nrow(xy2_hat), replace=TRUE) xy2_boot <- xy2_hat[b_id, ] reg2_b <- lm(Murder ~ Assault+UrbanPop, data=xy2_boot) boot_coefs2[b, ] <- coef(reg2_b) } colnames(boot_coefs2) <- names(coef(reg2)) # The bootstrap SE is just the standard deviation across replications apply(boot_coefs2, 2, sd) ## (Intercept) Assault UrbanPop ## 1.61167232 0.00468114 0.02707630 # The SEs are about 0.005 for Assault and 0.027 for UrbanPop. # So the UrbanPop coefficient, about -0.045, lies within two SEs of 0. # The joint distribution of the UrbanPop and Assault coefficients # Each point is one bootstrap replicate boot_coef2_df <- as.data.frame(cbind( ID=seq(nrow(boot_coefs2)), boot_coefs2)) fig2 <- plotly::plot_ly(boot_coef2_df, type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers', x = ~ UrbanPop, y = ~ Assault, text = ~ paste(' bootstrap dataset: ', ID, '', '
Coef. UrbanPop :', round(UrbanPop, 3), '
Coef. Assault :', round(Assault, 3), '

Intercept :', round(`(Intercept)`, 3)), hoverinfo='text', showlegend=FALSE, marker=list( color='rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)')) fig2 <- plotly::layout(fig2, showlegend=FALSE, title='Joint Bootstrap Distribution of Coefficients', xaxis = list(title='UrbanPop Coefficient'), yaxis = list(title='Assault Coefficient')) fig2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The cloud tilts down: the two coefficients tend to move in opposite ways. # Their correlation across replicates is about -0.5. ``` ::: ::: #### **F-statistic** {-} For a single coefficient we have the $t$-statistic; with several restrictions at once we need an analog that combines them into one number. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} The *$F$-statistic* compares the residual sum of squares of a restricted and an unrestricted model, scaled by their degrees of freedom. With $q$ restrictions, residual sum of squares $\hat{\text{RSS}} = \sum_{i} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}})^2$, and degrees of freedom $k_{u}$ unrestricted and $k_{r}$ restricted, $$\hat{F}_{q} = \frac{(\hat{\text{RSS}}_{r}-\hat{\text{RSS}}_{u})/(k_{u}-k_{r})}{\hat{\text{RSS}}_{u}/(n-k_{u})}.$$ ::: The $F$-statistic is useful for testing whether several restrictions on a regression hold simultaneously, by comparing two nested models with one number. The most common such test asks whether $K$ coefficients are all zero. A large $\hat{F}$ means the unrestricted model fits much better than the restricted one, beyond what would be expected by chance. The restrictions do not have to set coefficients to zero [@Wald1943; @Engle1984]. If you test whether all $K$ variables are jointly significant, the restricted model is a simple intercept and $\hat{\text{RSS}}_{r}=\hat{\text{TSS}}$, and $\hat{F}_{q}$ can be written in terms of $\hat{R}^2$: $\hat{F}_{K} = \frac{\hat{R}^2}{1-\hat{R}^2} \frac{n-K-1}{K}$. The first fraction is the relative goodness of fit, and the second fraction is an adjustment for degrees of freedom (similar to how we adjusted the $\hat{R}^2$ term before). We can also write this test statistic for whether all variables are statistically significant in terms of the adjusted $\hat{R}^2$: $$ \hat{F}_{K} = \frac{K + (n-K-1)\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}}{K(1 - \hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}})} $$ Notice that $\hat{F}_{K}=1$ when $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}=0$, meaning the model does not improve fit beyond what random covariates would achieve. The F-statistic exceeds $1$ when $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}>0$ and falls below $1$ when $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}<0$. :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Suppose $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}=0.50$, $K=2$, $n=50$. Then $$\hat{F}_{K} = \frac{K + (n-K-1)\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}}{K(1 - \hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}})} = \frac{2 + (50-2-1)(0.50)}{2(1-0.50)} = \frac{2+23.5}{2 \times 0.5} = \frac{25.5}{1} = 25.5.$$ This is well above $1$, indicating that the model explains substantially more variation than random covariates. You can verify: `qf(0.95, 2, 47)` $\approx 3.20$, so $\hat{F}_{K} = 25.5$ is highly significant. ::: :::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"} The `anova()` function compares two nested models with an F-test. Here we test whether `exper` adds explanatory power beyond `school`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reg_r <- lm(wage ~ school, data=xy_hat) # restricted reg_u <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat) # unrestricted anova(reg_r, reg_u) ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Model 1: wage ~ school ## Model 2: wage ~ school + exper ## Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) ## 1 3292 32386 ## 2 3291 31974 1 411.31 42.335 8.859e-11 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 # Experience adds explanatory power: F is about 42 and the p-value is near 0. # RSS falls only about 1 percent, but 3294 workers make that drop decisive. ``` ::: The F-statistic compares the drop in $\hat{\text{RSS}}$ to the adjusted mean squared error of the unrestricted model, $\hat{s}^2_{\text{adj}}=\hat{\text{RSS}}_{u}/(n-k_{u})$. A large F (small p-value) means the extra variable improves the fit by more than random noise would. ::: To conduct a hypothesis test, use a [permutation test](02_12_TwoGroups.qmd#permutation-tests): randomly reshuffle the outcomes, recompute the F statistic each time, and then compare how often shuffled data give something as extreme as your initial statistic. Shuffling the outcome across observations keeps each observation's covariates together, but breaks the link between the outcome and both covariates, which imposes the null. Here we test whether both slope coefficients are jointly zero in the model above, using the $\hat{F}_{K}$ that `summary()` reports. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE # Observed F-statistic, testing whether school and exper are jointly zero F_hat <- summary(reg)$fstatistic['value'] # Null distribution: shuffle the outcome to break its link with both covariates F_perm <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(F_perm)){ # Permuted data xy_perm <- xy_hat xy_perm$wage <- sample(xy_perm$wage, replace=FALSE) # Run regression and store the F-statistic reg_b <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_perm) F_perm[b] <- summary(reg_b)$fstatistic['value'] } hist(F_perm, xlim=c(0, F_hat*1.1), breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab=expression(hat(F)[b])) # Compare to initial statistic abline(v=F_hat, lwd=2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)) p_perm <- mean(F_perm >= F_hat) title(paste0('Permutation F-test: p = ', round(p_perm, 3)), font.main=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The observed F, about 166, lies far in the right tail. # The largest of the 399 shuffled F-statistics is only about 5. ``` ::: Under the null the F-statistic is small, averaging about $1$ as the formula above predicts when the covariates add nothing. :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Repeat both tests with `USArrests`. First use `anova()` to test whether `UrbanPop` adds explanatory power beyond `Assault`. Then run the permutation test of `Assault` and `UrbanPop` jointly in `Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop`. How can the two tests point in different directions? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Second dataset: arrests per 100,000 residents in the 50 US states, 1973 xy2_hat <- USArrests reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault+UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat) # Test UrbanPop alone, given Assault reg2_r <- lm(Murder ~ Assault, data=xy2_hat) # restricted reg2_u <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat) # unrestricted anova(reg2_r, reg2_u) ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Model 1: Murder ~ Assault ## Model 2: Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop ## Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) ## 1 48 331.85 ## 2 47 312.87 1 18.977 2.8507 0.09796 . ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 # UrbanPop adds little beyond Assault: F is about 2.9 and the p-value about 0.1. # Observed F-statistic for both coefficients jointly F2_hat <- summary(reg2)$fstatistic['value'] # Shuffling Murder keeps each state's Assault and UrbanPop together. # It breaks the link with both covariates, which imposes the null. F2_perm <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(F2_perm)){ # Permuted data xy2_perm <- xy2_hat xy2_perm$Murder <- sample(xy2_perm$Murder, replace=FALSE) # Run regression and store the F-statistic reg2_b <- lm(Murder ~ Assault+UrbanPop, data=xy2_perm) F2_perm[b] <- summary(reg2_b)$fstatistic['value'] } hist(F2_perm, xlim=c(0, F2_hat*1.1), breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab=expression(hat(F)[b])) # Compare to initial statistic abline(v=F2_hat, lwd=2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)) p2_perm <- mean(F2_perm >= F2_hat) title(paste0('Permutation F-test: p = ', round(p2_perm, 3)), font.main=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The observed joint F, about 46, lies far in the right tail. # Assault alone already fits well, so the joint test rejects. # The test of UrbanPop alone asks only about what it adds beyond Assault. ``` ::: ::: Note that *hypothesis testing is not to be done routinely*, as additional complications arise when testing multiple hypothesis sequentially. Under some additional assumptions $F_{q}$ follows an [F-distribution](01_09_AdvancedProbability.qmd#f). For more about F-testing, see and ## Coefficient Interpretation Notice that we have gotten pretty far without actually trying to meaningfully interpret regression coefficients. That is because the above procedure will always give us a number, regardless of whether the true data generating process is linear or not. So, to be cautious, we have been interpreting the regression outputs while being agnostic as to how the data are generated. We now consider a special situation where we know the data are generated according to a linear process and are only uncertain about the parameter values. If the data generating process is truly linear then we have a famous result that lets us attach a simple interpretation of OLS coefficients as unbiased estimates of the effect of each $X_{ik}$. For example, generate a simulated dataset with $30$ observations and two exogenous variables. Assume the following relationship: $Y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{i1} + \beta_{2} X_{i2} + \epsilon_{i}$ where the variables and the error term are realizations of the following data generating processes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} N <- 30 beta_true <- c(10, 2, -1) x1_sim <- runif(N, 0, 5) x2_sim <- rbinom(N, 1, .7) X <- cbind(1, x1_sim, x2_sim) e <- rnorm(N, 0, 3) y_sim <- X%*%beta_true + e xy_sim <- data.frame(y_sim, X) coef(lm(y_sim ~ x1_sim+x2_sim, data=xy_sim)) ## (Intercept) x1_sim x2_sim ## 10.5710560 1.9817680 -0.9137669 ``` ::: Simulate the distribution of coefficients under a correctly specified model. Interpret the average. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE N <- 30 beta_true <- c(10, 2, -1) Coefs <- matrix(NA, nrow=3, ncol=400) for(sim in 1:400){ x1_sim_b <- runif(N, 0, 5) x2_sim_b <- rbinom(N, 1, .7) X <- cbind(1, x1_sim_b, x2_sim_b) e <- rnorm(N, 0, 3) y_sim_b <- X%*%beta_true + e xy_sim_b <- data.frame(y_sim_b, x1_sim_b, x2_sim_b) Coefs[, sim] <- coef(lm(y_sim_b ~ x1_sim_b+x2_sim_b, data=xy_sim_b)) } par(mfrow=c(1, 2)) for(i in 2:3){ hist(Coefs[i, ], breaks=50, xlab=bquote(beta[.(i-1)]), main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE) abline(v=mean(Coefs[i, ]), lwd=2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)) abline(v=beta_true[i], col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Many economic phenomena are nonlinear, even when including potential transforms of $\hat{y}$ and $\hat{x}_{k}$. Sometimes the linear model may still be a good or even great approximation. But sometimes not, and it is hard to know ex-ante. Examine the distribution of coefficients under this misspecified model and try to interpret the average. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## MAIN EXAMPLE N <- 30 Coefs <- matrix(NA, nrow=3, ncol=600) for(sim in 1:600){ x2_sim_b <- runif(N, 0, 5) x3_sim_b <- rbinom(N, 1, .7) e <- rnorm(N, 0, 3) y_sim_b <- 10*x3_sim_b + 2*log(x2_sim_b)^x3_sim_b + e xy_sim_b <- data.frame(y_sim_b, x2_sim_b, x3_sim_b) Coefs[, sim] <- coef(lm(y_sim_b ~ x2_sim_b+x3_sim_b, data=xy_sim_b)) } par(mfrow=c(1, 2)) for(i in 2:3){ hist(Coefs[i, ], breaks=50, xlab=bquote(beta[.(i)]), main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE) abline(v=mean(Coefs[i, ]), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_22_MultipleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: In the misspecified case there is no true $\beta$ for OLS to recover, because the data are not generated by a linear model. The estimated coefficients still have a meaning: OLS returns the linear model that best approximates the true relationship in a least-squares sense. This is why we can still interpret them, cautiously, even when the linear model is wrong. :::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"} Compare the two simulation results. In the correctly specified case, the estimated coefficients center on the true values. What happens in the misspecified case? Why might OLS still be useful even when the model is misspecified? ::: In general, you can interpret your regression coefficients as *adjusted correlations*: the partial relationship between $\hat{y}$ and one $\hat{x}_{k}$ after netting out the linear dependence on the other explanatory variables. There are (many) tests for whether the relationships in your dataset are actually additively separable and linear. A simple way to let a relationship bend is to add the square of an explanatory variable as another regressor [@wooldridge2019]. #### **$\hat{R}^2$ vs. $\hat{b}$** {-} A small $\hat{R}^2$ does not mean your coefficients are useless. The two quantities answer [different questions](02_15_SimpleRegression.qmd#precision-and-fit): $\hat{b}_{k}$ tells us how $\hat{y}$ moves with $\hat{x}_{k}$, holding other regressors fixed, while $\hat{R}^2$ tells us how much of the variation in $\hat{y}$ the model captures. If most of the variation in $\hat{y}$ comes from things outside the model, $\hat{R}^2$ will be small even when $\hat{b}_{k}$ is precisely estimated. For example, wage regressions on years of schooling often report $\hat{R}^2$ around $0.1$, yet the schooling coefficient is one of the most studied quantities in labor economics. That said, we still care about $\hat{R}^2$. A very small $\hat{R}^2$ can signal that the model is misspecified (missing important variables or interactions, nonlinear relationships). In this case, you are not actually estimating a theoretical parameter.^[Even if the model is correctly specified, we will care about $R^2$. The unexplained variance affects standard errors, so smaller $\hat{R}^2$ typically widens confidence intervals. Alternatively, if you want to forecast $\hat{y}$, a small $\hat{R}^2$ means wide prediction intervals.] ## Exercises 1.
